title: Prevention and support

blocks.heading: Prevention and support
blocks.text: Responses can combine prevention, accountable protection and accessible health and social support. Match the actual barrier, such as unsafe disclosure or transport, to a qualified implementer. A campaign alone may not make an existing service reachable.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Responses to GBV
blocks.text:
Education about respectful relationships, safe reporting routes and survivor-centred professional support can form complementary responses. Confidentiality, safety and non-blaming treatment matter to usable access. A learner should seek help from a trusted responsible adult or qualified service rather than investigate a disclosure.

Applied example: Education can challenge norms that excuse abuse and promote respectful relationships. Accessible professional protection and support can help survivors obtain safety and assistance.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Responses to baby dumping
blocks.text:
Accessible, non-stigmatising pregnancy, parenting, health and social support can address crises and barriers to help. Qualified services must handle immediate safety and child-protection needs. The lesson teaches prevention and referral principles, not current legal advice or instructions for relinquishing a child.

Applied example: Confidential pregnancy and parenting support can help a person seek help before a crisis escalates. Assistance with continued education or financial hardship can reduce specific pressures while protecting the child.

blocks.heading: A practical access test
blocks.text: In a fictional support programme, a nearby trained adviser offers confidential appointments and explains referral options. This may help people seek assistance earlier, but consent, privacy and continued service capacity still matter. Prevention and support need complementary actions; telling people to seek help is insufficient if the route is unsafe, unavailable or unaffordable.

blocks.heading: Distinct prevention and support responses
blocks.text: Responses to GBV can include challenging norms that excuse abuse, improving equal access to income and education, teaching respectful relationships, providing safe reporting routes, and making professional protection and survivor support reachable. Public institutions, trained health and social workers, schools and community organisations have different responsibilities. Preventing baby dumping can include confidential pregnancy and parenting support, assistance to remain in education, reliable information on voluntary family planning, and help with financial or emotional crises. A response should remove a stated barrier and protect the infant; shame or exposure can deter help. These are educational support principles, not instructions for a learner to investigate violence or manage an emergency alone.
